candidates.above_next: It states the language's deepest stance on correctness and touches more code than first-classness, which is structural but quieter in daily use.

also.why: it reframes an error as a first-class outcome to raise rather than a sentinel value the caller must guess at

beats.why: l75 only laments that uncaught type errors slip through; it diagnoses the harm but never states the rule

harms: forces handling of exceptions throughout the code
halts on conditions another language would tolerate
runtime cost of the checks that raise
candidates.quote: I decided that there should be no undefined result values in L – instead, exceptions should always be raised when no correct return value can be computed.
candidates.statement: When no correct value can be computed, raise an exception; never return an undefined value or let an error pass silently.

strongest.why: it fixes a stance that a language must never hand back a wrong-looking value; it refuses to let a computation run on nonsense

candidates.above_next: Equal status of all objects reorganizes the whole type model, outranking the syntactic discipline of C3 which is a means rather than a worldview.

also.why: economy: one rule, equal status, no exceptions to carve out

beats.why: l53 applies the same idea to one case, the type object, so it infects less than the general rule

harms: uniform object overhead even for small values like integers
no privileged primitives, harder to optimize
candidates.quote: In L, all objects that can be named are said to be "first class."
candidates.statement: Every object that can be named has equal status: it can be assigned, passed, returned and stored like any other.

strongest.why: it collapses the hierarchy between values so one mental model covers integers, functions, classes and modules alike

candidates.above_next: The refusal to grow syntax guides more concrete decisions than dynamic typing, which is one choice made once.

also.why: the grammar stays small; one rule covers many cases

beats.why: l101 names the same cut-corners instinct but as a self-deprecating story about classes, not as a rule to follow

harms: overloading one construct for many roles can surprise users
cut corners leave semantic gaps fixed only later
power hidden behind conventions rather than visible syntax
candidates.quote: A major design constraint was that I didn't want to add syntax for methods that differed from the syntax for functions.
candidates.statement: Prefer the minimal solution that reuses existing mechanisms; do not add new syntax when an existing construct will serve.

strongest.why: a discipline that resists growing the language: solve by reusing what exists before inventing syntax

candidates.above_next: Names-refer-to-objects reframes assignment itself, above the repr round-trip which is narrower.

also.why: no declarations, less ceremony to write

beats.why: l42 is a consequence of this choice (no going back once chosen), not the choice itself

harms: type errors surface only at run time
silent wrong results when the wrong type is passed
candidates.quote: In L, variables are simply names that refer to objects.
candidates.statement: Variables are names that refer to objects, needing no declaration; all type checking happens at run time.

strongest.why: a variable is not a box holding a typed value but a name bound to an object; this rebinds how one thinks about assignment and identity

candidates.above_next: The print/parse invariant is a vivid aesthetic rule, slightly above the more abstract call to generalize types.

also.why: it ties the printed form to the grammar, making the language its own serialization

beats.why: l142 is about what the parser does and doesn't know of a convention, a narrower observation than the print/parse invariant

harms: not every object has a sensible literal form, forcing awkward or fake reprs
the round-trip promise is hard to keep for complex objects
candidates.quote: One of the rules I took from the predecessor was that every data type, when printed or converted to a string, should be represented by an expression that was a valid input to the language's parser.
candidates.statement: Every value, when printed or converted to a string, should read back as a valid expression to the parser.

strongest.why: a clean round-trip invariant: what you print, you can read back

candidates.above_next: Generalization reorganizes the type system, while hiding implementation details guides fewer decisions.

also.why: economy: length, indexing, slicing and iteration defined once

beats.why: l134 is one beautiful instance of the slicing design, not the general move to abstract a common concept

harms: forcing disparate types under one concept can hide meaningful differences
the abstraction may leak for types that don't fit
candidates.quote: I decided to generalize these to a common concept, the sequence.
candidates.statement: Generalize related types to a common concept so core operations work the same on all of them.

strongest.why: it finds the shared structure, the sequence, so one set of operations works across list, tuple and string

also.why: it shifts the boundary of what the programmer must hold in mind

beats.why: l1 celebrates conciseness as a result, but doesn't say which way to decide when a detail could leak to the user

harms: hiding details can cost performance the user cannot control
users lose a mental model of what the machine does
candidates.quote: the predecessor-inspired philosophy of not requiring users to care about a uninteresting implementation details
candidates.statement: Do not require users to care about uninteresting implementation details.

strongest.why: a stance that users should not be burdened with implementation concerns that don't interest them
